speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: USE OF CANADIAN HIGHWAYS BY UNITED STATES TRUCKS CARRYING WAR MATERIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I saw in
the Ottawa Journal the article to which my hon. friend refers. The subject matter has been outstanding for a long time. A project was undertaken, I think in 1937, to provide for the movement of United States traffic from' Buffalo to Detroit via Canadian highways. The project at that time was and, so far as I know is, at present that a fleet of Canadian trucks would be built and would operate with Canadian gasoline between points across two international boundaries. A bill was introduced in the Senate during the session of 1938 by the sponsors of the project, and the project has been revived from time to time since then. I cannot say why I was selected as the bottleneck, for the matter is not one related to the Ministry of Munitions and Supply, which is my present portfolio, or to the Ministry of Transport, which was my former portfolio. I suppose I figure in the matter only as one member of the government. I may say, however, that the representations have always come from parties interested either in building the trucks or in selling the gasoline or operating a toll bridge or toll tunnel. I have never seen representations from potential users of the service.
We have petitions, signed, I think by every village along the route protesting against this type of traffic on the highways, and I think the reason is obvious: the highways are too narrow for that sort of traffic if the residents alongside are to be permitted to live. subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, March 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacKinnon (Edmonton West) for the second reading of Bill No. 13, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Douglas (Weyburn).

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to detain the house very long with my remarks this afternoon. I feel, however, that I should say a few words in view of the fact that some of my friends on the left have seen fit, since I spoke on the motion itself, to mention my name from time to time.
First of all I should like to express appreciation to hon. members from other parts of Canada who have spoken on this question. Although all of them have not entirely agreed with the requests which have come from western Canada, they have shown a desire to examine those requests fairly and to do what they regard as a measure of justice to fellow Canadians who live in the west. I am sure that that attitude is very much appreciated by western members.
I realize, of course, that there is a feeling that when you put the assistance granted by parliament on a bushel basis entirely, you lay yourself open to the charge which is made from time to time by hon. members from other parts of the country, that the larger the scale upon which a man farms, or
Wheat Board Act

the bigger his crop, the more you give him, and the smaller the farm he has, or the poorer his crop, the less you give him. I have heard many hon. members from the east say that they would not mind giving all necessary assistance to a man to live and bring up his family, but they do object to giving large sums of money to people who mine wheat and produce thousands and thousands of bushels.
That brings up something which should always be borne in mind by those of us who come from western Canada. Last fall there was quite a movement to make a further payment on participation certificates which had been given to farmers who had delivered wheat last fall to the wheat board. The suggestion was made that at least another 10 cents be paid, which would have cost the government $20 million. I was one who urged very strongly that, if the government were ready to pay $20 million to assist western agriculture, it would be much fairer to pay that out on an acreage basis than by means of a further 10 cents a bushel on wheat delivered to the wheat board.
In my own constituency, I believe the average yield would not be more than around six bushels to the acre. There was an almost entire failure of coarse grains in some parts of it, which meant that the people in that constituency, after they took out two bushels an acre for seed, provided for their own flour requirements, and kept back wheat for feeding purposes to take the place of the oats and barley which they did not have, would have very little wheat to sell. Furthermore, about half the people in western Canada who did have wheat to sell had sold it on the open market. So, if you had granted 10 cents a bushel, very little money would have gone into constituencies like mine; all the money would have gone to those districts which had good crops.
So far as I was concerned I said, if the treasury of this country is going to devote $20 million to assist the farmers of western Canada, if it puts it out on an acreage basis it is going to make sure that everybody gets something, and that the person with no cron or a poor crop gets at least as much as the person with a good crop. Surely that is not unfair.
But, Mr. Speaker, because I took that stand, and had to oppose the suggestion that that ten cents should be paid out on wheat, I was attacked by those people from the heavy crop districts who wanted the price paid on wheat, and who demanded it, and were ready to try to destroy anybody who would not fall in line with that view.

So far as I am concerned, I have no apologies for the stand I took. I believe that if the money which this parliament is ready to vote for the assistance of western Canada were placed at least in part upon an acreage basis, rather than used in an attempt to run up the price without regard to helping the man with no crop or a low crop, there would be far more support for that proposal in this house than there is for a high price for wheat alone.
As I stated in my speech on the main motion, agriculture is as much entitled to parity prices as is any other branch of industry or activity in this country. There are two ways in which you can grant parity prices. I took 1913-14 as the base and indicated that to give the farmer the same purchasing power as he had in that year he would have to receive the equivalent of $1.20 a' bushel, basis No. 1 northern. In 1913-14 there were no bonus payments. There was nothing of that sort. But if you give an initial price and then supplement it with bonus payments which raise the average amount received by the farmer to the equivalent of $1.20 a bushel basis No. 1 northern, Fort William, you are really giving parity prices although it does not appear so on the surface. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) pointed out in his very able speech-in fact there were two of them, and I enjoyed them very much; I hope they will be sent all over western Canada; I intend to do my part to see that they are-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: They will be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Thank you very much. He pointed out that on the basis of 70 cents initial payment, Fort William, and another $60 million spread over 200 million bushels, the price was brought up to $1 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William; that is the average amount received by the farmer. If this motion carries and the initial price is raised to 90 cents a bushel; if the government could see its way clear to make the same bonus payments this year as it made last year, * and if, further, the crop were the same size, 200 million bushels, then it would raise to the parity or basic price, the average price, namely, $1.20 a bushel basis No. 1 northern, Fort William. But by doing it in that way you would be making sure that the person with a low crop or a short crop got something. In that regard of course I will admit that if we grow enough wheat to market the 280 million bushels of which the government considers receiving delivery, the amount of these bonuses spread over 280 million bushels would represent only 22 cents a bushel-not quite that- and so raise the average price received by the farmer to $1.12 instead of $120. That would be only if you continued the prairie farm

Wheat Board Act
assistance payments, .the wheat acreage reduction payments and the prairie farm income payments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Under the other two bills as they are at present, the payments are cut in half. There would be no prairie farm assistance payment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend had waited, I was going to deal with that. I was going to point out that so far as I am concerned I should like to see the government provide for prairie farm assistance payments as large as were given last year, if not larger. I should like to see the bonus payments, that is prairie farm income payments, made as large as they were last year, if not larger. I think we in western Canada would be doing more good to the people who need it out west if we based our request to the government on that consideration instead of putting emphasis entirely upon price per bushel. My hon. friend says there is no provision for prairie farm income. There was no provision for prairie farm income when parliament adjourned last year; that was provided for by order in council. I sincerely hope that when the government by this bill is providing more money for those who have wheat to sell, it will not give less to the person with little or no wheat. Personally I am prepared to accept the provision in this bill for raising the price to only 90 cents a bushel, if supplemented by at least the same amount in bonus payments as made last year-1941. I wish to impress upoan the government, with all the emphasis I am capable of, that they do consider making the same bonus payments they made last year. If we have only 200 million bushels of wheat, it will bring the price up to $1.20; but even if they make the same bonus payments as they did last year and we deliver 280 millions bushels, then the price that will be received by the farmer will be around $1.12 basis No. 1 northern, Fort William.
One of the reasons why I am prepared to vote for this motion and have the matter referred to a committee is that all these considerations should, I think, be taken into account. On that committee there are Canadians from other parts of the dominion, who, I believe, want to see a measure of justice given the western farmers, and I trust that there will come out of the committee recommendations on the basis of which the government will see fit to make, and will be justified in making, bonus payments that will at least provide for the same amount paid by way of bonus as was paid last year.
This would mean an amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I hope that
these things will be given consideration. If the members of this house would take that attitude as a united group from western Canada, they would be doing more good for the farmers than by simply laying the entire emphasis on price. I have here a little table which I made up comparing receipts as between $1 a bushel and 90 cents a bushel with 1941 bonus payments. If we get 90 cents a bushel plus the bonus payments of last year, leaving out of consideration wheat acreage reduction-I am assuming in all cases the farmer will retain two bushels per acre for seed and that the price he receives on the farm is 20 cents under the amount received at Fort William-then in the nothing to four bushels per acre category, if the price were set at $1 the amount received by the farmer without bonuses, in that category, would be on the average nothing, because the average yield would be two bushels, which he would have to keep for seed. He would have nothing to sell, and no matter what this government granted as a price, such a man would get nothing at all from them- nothing on acreage and nothing per bushei. On the other hand, if the same bonus payments were made as last year, the average amount paid to the farmer in that category would be $2.75 an acre or $3.25 an acre if he were in a crop failure area. The amount per bushel cannot be calculated. It would be 275 times or 325 times what he had to sell, but he has nothing to sell, and so you cannot calculate the amount per bushel.
In the four to eight bushels per acre category, if you gave $1 a bushel without bonus, the amount he would get would be $3.20 an acre on the average, or 80 cents a bushel. But under the policy of 90 cents a bushel plus bonus he would get $5.05 an acre, which is almost $2 more, or an average of $1,261 a bushel instead of 80 cents. That is the position of the man in the four to eight bushels per acre category. Surely he is entitled to more help than the man with a large crop, and under this system he would receive $1.26i instead of 80 cents, as I have pointed out.
Take next the man with a yield of from eight to twelve bushels per acre. Under the dollar system and no bonus he would get $6.40 an acre, or 80 cents a bushel. But under the system of paying 90 cents plus bonus he would get $8.35 an acre as against $6.40, or $1.04 instead of 80 cents. So that even the man having from eight to twelve bushels to the acre is better off; in fact anybody getting less than twelve bushels to the acre would be better off to get 90 cents plus the same bonus as last year.
Wheat Board Act

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Has anyone in this debate, or the representative of any group, recommended that the bonus should not be paid?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: No. Apparently I have not made my point clear. It is that the amendment was made on the question of price. I think hon. members would have done better for western Canada and got more support in the rest of Canada if they had put the emphasis on asking for the same bonus or increasing the bonus. That, as I say, would have done more good to the people out west who need it and would have gained more support in the rest of Canada. Instead of that, the opposition moved an amendment based entirely on the question of price. I leave it to the judgment of this house and of western Canada as to why they placed the emphasis on price instead of on what would be in the best interests of our country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: The hon. member could have moved an amendment to that effect.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Yes, but I am not in the opposition. I will deal with that in a moment. The function of an opposition I think is not to play to the gallery but to do the best thing for their people out west.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I object to that imputation of motives that in doing a perfectly legitimate and proper thing we were playing to the gallery. I ask that that aspersion be withdrawn.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I think the hon. member should withdraw that statement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I withdraw it. As a matter of fact I would not have said it if I had not been goaded on.
Now take those in the category from twelve to twenty bushels. It is when one gets into that category that he is better off if given a dollar a bushel without bonus. Then he gets an average of $11.20 an acre, or 80 cents a bushel, whereas under the system of bonus and 90 cents a bushel, it would yield only $10.55 an acre.
That is the comparative effect of the two systems. In my judgment my hon. friends would have done better to put a little more emphasis upon bonuses for the benefit of the farmer with the poor crop or no crop at all.
A question was raised about amendments and so on. I spoke Monday last about the effect of the raising of the price to 90 cents on the person in the eight to twelve bushels per acre category. I urged the minister to consider an amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to make sure the person in that 
category would get $1 an acre on half of his acreage. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how many hon. members of the opposition supported me in that view?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I did.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I believe the hon. member for Weyburn did, and I give him credit, but how many others did?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: He spoke for the group.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Well, we will give the group credit, but another member of the group did not mention it when he spoke.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: We do not repeat things.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Oh, I think if there is any group in the house that does repeat, it is the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group. If they had felt very strongly about this, they would not have minded repeating it- every one of them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: We have not finished yet. There is still the committee stage.	.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Well, you might have done it in the house too. I shall be glad, however, if you accept the suggestion and support it in committee for all you are worth.
The question before the house is a simple one of approving the principle that we raise the initial price from 70 cents to- 90 cents. To that the hon. member for Weyburn has moved an amendment, the effective part of which reads as follows:
That this bill be not now read a second time-
That is the bill raising the price from 70 to 90 cents.
-but be it resolved that the disregarding by this parliament of the modest representations made by western agriculture for a parity price for all agricultural products and an initial wheat payment of at least $1 per bushel for No. 1 northern basis Fort William is contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada.
That amendment is sufficiently comprehensive that if my hon. friends had been much interested in the bonus, they could have introduced a suggestion that they were favourable to its partly being achieved at least by a bonus plan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: The legislation provides that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
The foundation is well laid in western Canada for my hon. friends to get a great deal of credit by coming out for dollar wheat. I will not say that was the reason for moving this amendment, but it will be for the people of western Canada to judge when the time comes.

Wheat Board Act
What would be the effect of voting for this amendment? It would be that the attempt to raise the price from 70 cents to 90 cents would be defeated.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Of course it would be. The motion for second reading would be defeated. The bill would be killed. It would not go to committee. Who would revive that bill? Unless the government were ready to bring in another bill, it would be killed and the price would remain at 70 cents.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: It is an awful reflection.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
There are enough hon.
members in this house who do not believe in raising the price over 70 cents that if my hon. friends joined them in voting that way and against the bill, it would be defeated and we would not get another cent over 70 cents. Yet they decry the very policy that makes it possible for us in the west to get a little measure of justice. Again, Mr. Speaker, I leave it to the judgment of the country whether or not they believe those things they have been saying. I am not saying they do not, because of course if I did so I would be made to withdraw it.
Suppose we take another possibility. Supposing the government were to say, This is a question of confidence, of government policy, and we expect our members, the government as a whole having agreed upon it, to back us us up in doing what we think is best for the country as a whole, and to vote for it. And supposing all of us from western Canada, regardless of party, including the Liberal members were to join in attempting to defeat the government and were to carry the amendment killing a bill brought in by a minister; it would bring on an election in this country at this time. Does anyone suppose that if we forced an election on an issue which has to do only with making us in western Canada better off, we would get from such an election as sympathetic a parliament as we have to-day? After all, we must face realities. I know my hon. friends will say, "We can take the stand that you are not doing enough, because the government, having made it a question of government policy, has enough supporters to put it through. The increase from 70 cents to 90 cents will not be stopped. So we can fight it and oppose it; the Liberals will have to take the onus of putting it through. We can move an amendment like this, then we can go out into the country and say that the Liberals have done so and so, and we can read their names." They will read the names of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner), perhaps; the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven), and, if you will, the member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). I have read in the papers over and over again how my hon. friends have suggested that that dirty dog from Rosthern has voted against the best interests of the farmers of the west.

order. The hon. gentleman is imputing language to members of this house which they have never used.

has ever heard me, or any other member of this group, refer to anyone in that language. May I say also, on a further point of order, that the hon. gentleman is imputing to this group motives which he has no right to impute.

hear from the acting leader of the opposition

185,000	farmers of Saskatchewan who signed the petition, and which has the support of great numbers of farmers in Alberta and Manitoba. The statement made by the hon. member for Rosthern to-day, that those who would support this amendment would do so in order to play to the gallery, is very poor tribute to the great number of western farmers who believe that the only salvation for western agriculture lies in the adoption of the principle set out therein.
This is not a matter of charity. After listening to the hon. member for Rosthern one would almost think that hon. members from other parts of Canada feel that when 
western agriculture is assisted the government is doing an act of charity. I do not think that is their attitude; I have not found it to be that way. The western farmer to-day is not asking for charity but for parity, for equality with all other industries in Canada producing the needs of war, to the end that western agriculture, as well as agriculture generally throughout the dominion, may enjoy the same consideration that is given other industries in Canada to-day.
I am not one of those who contend that increasing the advance to 90 cents a bushel will not be advantageous to western Canada. It will. It is a step in the right direction. But I would point out that the problem, so far as the wheat grower is concerned, consists of two parts. First there is the problem of getting a fair and reasonable price to the farmer who has a crop; and then, there is the problem of giving a fair allowance or compensation to those who by reason of drought or otherwise, have not a sufficient crop. So far as this legislation is concerned, while it increases the initial payment by 20 cents a bushel, it takes away a very considerable amount from those who this year will not have a crop at all. It makes no provision for the payment of a prairie farm income, and it reduces the payment under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, in that those who have a crop of from eight to twelve bushels to the acre will be denied any bonus this year. What is the reason, I ask, for the change in point of view? It seems clear that it is not a question of any increased price being paid by the British government. Throughout the year 1941 the explanation was that the government could not set the price above 70 cents because Great Britain was not paying more. No one asks Great Britain to pay more, even should the principle of the amendment be accepted. Why has there been a change in policy? Was it Donald Gordon of the wartime prices and trade board who asked the government to make the change? The increase will interfere with the price ceiling-a price ceiling which we condemned last fall in this house, because it set the prices of agricultural products at one level and the prices of things the farmer had to buy at a higher level.
Last November, at the very time the Minister of Agriculture was making his statement to the press that the government did not believe in any increase in the initial payment, meetings were being held throughout western Canada asking for an initial price of SI, for a parity price, and for payment over a period of years of the difference between the amount of the initial advance and the amount of the parity price.
The hon. member for Rosthem pointed out-and with considerable force-the reason why hon. members supporting the government could not support some of the amendments moved by opposition members. May I point out, so far as the parity price is concerned, that on March 26 last an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) and seconded by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). The motion having been dropped, it was again placed on Hansard by myself, and seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). In that resolution the following words appeared1:
That the government should take immediate steps to create a parity of prices as between agricultural and other products in order to improve the condition of Canadian agriculture and in order that it may receive a just and fair return, and thus be enabled to make that contribution to Canada's war effort which is so desirable, and which our agricultural population so greatly desire to make.
A subamendment was moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson). It provided for a minimum price of 85 cents a bushel, a processing tax and certain other terms to which I shall not now refer. A resolution, upon which the subamendment was based, had been adopted by the Saskatchewan legislature unanimously.
When the matter came up for vote in the house why was it that every hon. member on the government side, except the hon.

member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) found it necessary to vote against those two amendments? They voted against the principle of the parity price, and voted against an increase to 85 cents in the initial payment to western farmers.
Hansard reports that the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) went out of his way last night to refer to me. I cannot say he voted against either of the amendments, because apparently he was not in the house at the time that one of the most important resolutions affecting western agriculture was being voted upon.
The initial payment of 90 cents a bushel apparently represents a compromise between those who believe that western Canada and the western farmer are receiving enough to-day and those who want the government to go the whole length; but I cannot understand why it is necessary for the government in making this compromise to do away in part with some of the bonuses which western Canada has been enjoying during the past year. The Minister of Agriculture has on more than one occasion referred with pride to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, as he is entitled to do, because it represented a very material advance in improving the economic position of the farmer. It has meant much to western Canada and I think it only fair to say that if it had not been for that legislation many of those in my constituency who are able at least to carry on during 1942 would have been quite unable to do so.

They did not come in any threatening manner; they came in an attitude of compromise because they had been unable to obtain what they have been asking for since 1935. bringing together east and west it might defeat the government. We on this side of the house have consistently stood for the things which this delegation of farmers stood for and the essence of what they stood for was a parity price, with an initial payment of $1 per bushel. They are now to receive 90 cents under the legislation, and they should know at the same time that while the government is raising the payment to 90 cents it is taking away from them certain of the bonuses which they are enjoying to-day.
I am not going into any figures to-day in reference to the increase in the cost of living or a comparison of the index of 1913-14 with 1941, because that has already been done. The war has been on for two and a half years. We have pressed for these things in season and out of season, and it is only now on the eve of a provincial election in the province of Saskatchewan that the government has seen fit to introduce legislation to improve the position of the western farmer.
I do not hear any denial of my statement that it is anticipated that there will be a provincial election this summer in Saskatchewan. I am going to say this, and I know it will not appeal to all hon. members in this house, that with the war situation what it is to-day, and with the warning ringing in our ears which the Prime Minister gave the night before last as to the peril in which we find ourselves, no government in any province should find it necessary, particularly when it has still one year and a half to run, to go to the people and divide and separate them and have all the recriminations that necessarily accompany an election at the very time when Canada and the empire will be fighting our greatest battle for survival.
The government of the province of Saskatchewan has still one year and a half to go and if it calls an election this summer it will be calling it in a world situation described by the Prime Minister the day before yesterday in these words:
Never in the world's history has the danger to civilization itself been comparable to what it is at this very hour. Even in the short period since the launching of the loan, the enemy, on all fronts but one, has gained an almost continuous series of military successes. He is continuing to make further and far-reaching gains.
From every continent and from every ocean the call continues to come for more planes, more tanks, more munitions, more ships, more food, more fighting men.

speechtext:
I thought he had gone so far as to say that there was not going to be one. Well, he would know. I am making a serious appeal, Mr. Speaker, with respect to holding this provincial election in Saskatchewan, and what I say applies to every province, for this is a time as never before, as members of the house are fully aware, when we are in a position of great peril, with the enemy at our gates.
I shall not take up very much more time. I have a few recommendations and suggestions to make to the minister and I shall give them as shortly as I can. My first suggestion is that he carry out the request of the farm delegation. The recommendations that were made by these western farmers to a solution of their problems represented a minimum, and I would point out that even if $1 a bushel were fixed as the initial payment the farmer would still find himself receiving in purchasing power only about 78 cents a bushel as at the beginning of the war. Reading over the evidence that was given when this delegation was before the government I find that without exception the minister's attitude was that the government was going to do its very best. Then, Mr. Speaker, my suggestion even at this late hour is that the hope expressed by Mr. Wesson, that tribune of the western farmers,
Wheat Board Act

be carried into effect and that in committee the 90 cents a bushel initial payment be increased to SI.
Secondly, I respectfully suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act be amended so that farmers this year raising from eight to twelve bushels an acre will be enabled to receive a bonus.
Thirdly, a very striking address was made the other day in this house by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) in which he set out in detail the levy which is being made to-day by the great storage corporations upon agriculture in general, and the wheat farmers of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba in particular. I am not going to repeat what he said on that occasion, excepting to quote one statement he made, which appears at page 1183 of Hansard:
There is no doubt therefore the elevators will be receiving in the neighbourhood of at least $50,000,000 for the handling of grain this year. On the other hand what does the farmer get? He gets less than 50 cents a bushel for
200,000.000 bushels. He will not receive $100,000,000, yet here is a man who does not do anything except handling the wheat and he is getting half as much as the farmer.
I suggest that, having regard to the tremendous amounts of wheat which are stored, the time has come to reduce storage rates below one forty-fifth of a cent by at least 33 per cent.
To me it is difficult to understand why, when the government has control of practically ill the wheat in the dominion, it has seen fit ;o rent its terminal elevators to private corporations to store Canada's wheat, paying them one forty-fifth of a cent per bushel per day. On the 21st of May, 1941, I asked how many terminal or interior grain elevators in Canada and the United States were owned, leased or otherwise controlled by the government; where were such elevators located and what was their capacity. The answer of the Department of Trade and Commerce was that there are in Canada under the control of that department eight terminal elevators, located at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Lethbridge, Edmonton, Calgary, Prince Rupert and Port Arthur, with a total capacity of about 23,000,000 bushels one of which was rented to a private corporation and that the government received the year before as rentals $72,230.98. If one-forty-fifth of a cent a bushel was paid on the full capacity of the elevator-and they must have been full because there was such a shortage of storage- these companies received less of course the cost of administration, $260,000. I might point out too that ten elevators with a tremendous capacity, under the control of the Department of Transport, also are rented to private corporations, enabling those corporations to receive the tolls paid to them by the gov-
ernment for the storage of their own wheat. I think the time has come when the government of Canada should once more take over these elevators for the storage of the Canadian farmers wheat, instead of renting them to the private storage corporations, which are securing in consequence tremendous returns.
I suggest, next, that the time has come when we should again press for utilization of the Hudson Bay railway facilities. They have not been used to any extent since 1935. They have been used less, of course, since the war began-but very little less. My suggestion is that the whole problem of the Hudson Bay railway and the use of this particular route at this time should also be placed before the committee, to the end that the facilities which we have shall be utilized to the benefit of the people.
My next suggestion is this. Some weeks ago a speech was delivered in this chamber by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Turner) in which he suggested that the government should give consideration to the equalization of freight rates so that the . farmer living in far-off Alberta or northern Saskatchewan would be in an identical position with a farmer living in the province of Manitoba. The arguments that he advanced in that connection appealed to me, and I suggest that they should be placed before this committee when it meets.
Next: Britain closed her wheat exchange directly the war broke out. We on this side of the house without exception since the beginning of the war have advocated the closing of the exchange. There was a suggestion the other day that it was going to be closed, but that has not yet been imported into the terms of any order in council, as I have been able to read those orders in council which were issued on March 9. Let me say in that connection that I cannot understand the attitude of the government in bringing before parliament only part of this problem, and, with parliament in session, passing three orders in council dealing with flax, wheat and so on and empowering the government, in so far as one order in council is concerned, to do that for which they condemned1 Mr. McFarland and the Bennett government, namely, to purchase wheat from others than the actual owners and producers. For the last several years the government has condemned the action of the government of Mr. Bennett, yet now by order in council they ask power to do that which they have condemned.
What of the grain exchange? Is it to be closed? Is it to continue? I was interested the other day in listening to the address of

Wheat Board Act
the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) when he pointed out that trading in flax was to be forbidden. I asked him why, and the answer he gave was that the handling of flax is being made a monopoly of the Canadian wheat board in order to avoid speculative profits by people in possession of flax acquired at very much lower prices.
I ask, is the wheat situation any different in principle? The price of wheat is to be raised to 90 cents. Are there to be any provisions which will prevent those who acquired wheat at lower prices from selling it to-day at a profit. I would be glad to hear what they are.
The minister went on to say that a corresponding procedure has been adopted to prevent speculation in wheat for the same reason, and the house is entitled to details. Mr. Speaker, one thing which can be said for this government is that, if it has not been too favourable to the needs and the requirements of the producer, it has never failed to take cognizance of the needs of the storage and trading corporations. That is one of the major complaints made all over western Canada against this government.
I offer this as a further suggestion. When we are paying out, as the hon. member for Wood Mountain said, about $50,000,000 a year for storage, or half of what the farmer receives who produces the wheat, it is time to utilize the powers under the National Resources Mobilization Act, take over these elevators at a fair rental, or in any event those elevators which belong to the government, and operate them for the benefit of the farmers and taxpayers of Canada, instead of paying toll as at present to those who are the owners or lessees.
My next suggestion is this, that in addition to taking over grain storage facilities the government should, if necessary, also take over the processing and distribution concerns, unless the prices charged are kept to a minimum. They are doing it in other countries. Only recently an investigation took place in the United States, instituted by the American government, to ascertain how much of the dollar that was ultimately paid by the consumer for farm products in that country went to the farmer, and it was found that in 1940, which was one of the best years so far as farmers were concerned, in a list of 58 foodstuffs produced by the farm and bought by the average labouring man's family, for which the consumer paid $314, $182 went to the middle man while the farmer received $132. In other words the farmer received 42 per cent of the price which the product, produced by himself, ultimately realized. That
was stated by Mr. R. O. Been, one of the authorities in the United States government, who said:
Any reduction in marketing charges should benefit the consumer through reducing retail prices, and improve the position of the farmer by increasing the prices which he receives. Reduction of marketing costs could result from breaking up congestion and increasing efficiency at certain points in the marketing process. Improvement of terminal market facilities is a step in this direction.
I come now to one of the most serious situations in agriculture to-day, the assuring to the farmer of a supply of necessary labour in operating his farm. The attractions of industry and of munitions factories in eastern Canada, and in western Canada the armed services themselves, have placed the farmer in the position where he will not be able to carry on unless something is done by the government. A step was taken in the right direction yesterday by the order in council placed before the house by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) whereby any man in the service may be granted leave so that he may assist with spring work and whereby national boards in the various provinces may grant the necessary postponements of men on farms who are called up for service.
The farmer is not asking that discrimination be made in his favour, but he feels that after two and a half years of war it is time that men were allocated to the positions and industries wherein they can do the most good. Allocations should be made of men from industries to farms, where they can better serve in that capacity, under a selective basis whereby all men should be placed where they can devote themselves to the best of their ability to the welfare of the state. In Britain it has been found necessary not only to comb munitions industries, but also to mobilize the young men and women in that nation to assist in agriculture. My suggestion is that the government at this time should consider the question of bringing in under the selective service provision the mobilization of the land army in Canada in order to ensure that the necessary production of food will continue.
It cannot be too often repeated that food is as necessary as munitions. Without food there can be no munitions, without food there can be no soldiers in the field. One of the major duties of the government at this time is to make sure this spring that farm labour shall be made available to farmers all over the dominion to the end that they shall be able to produce as they desire to do and whereby the empire's needs will be satisfied. Food is important. Only the other day I came across a quotation from the Secretary
Wheat Board Act

of Agriculture of the United States, Claude R. Wickard, which struck me as being so appropriate at this time that I will quote it, and with this quotation I will close:
Food is a whole arsenal of weapons in this struggle for human freedom. It is the driving force behind high production by munitions workers and top notch performance and strong morale among soldiers and sailors. Our national self-interest and our humanitarian instincts challenge us to do this job of producing food and do it on a scale that will write history. In the day of victory when the nations sit down at the peace table our food stocks will give great force to our views for they will show once and for all that democracy builds for the needs of common men. By winning our American battle of farm production we will help to make it possible once again for men in all parts of the earth to live in comfort, in tolerance and in freedom.

Mr. Speaker, in my view this is a problem that affects agriculture not only in western Canada but in other parts of the dominion as well, and for that reason I should like to make a few casual comments upon the subject. Representing as I do, feebly perhaps but to the best of >my ability, a riding in southwestern Ontario, a farming district, I regard this as a question of vital importance. Let me say at the outset that I am not in any way antagonistic to the people of western Canada or to western farm problems. I remember after speaking last year in the house I received *from western Canada certain communications commenting on what I had said and virtually accusing me of being an opponent of western agricultural problems. That is not true, because I am quite familiar with our own agricultural problems. In fact I have a good deal in common with and a great deal of sympathy for the people who derive their livelihood from farming, and I do not know of any time, apart from the last war, when they received very much for the commodities they produce.
I am not an authority on western problems. I am not an authority on the wheat situation as it affects the west. I was greatly interested last Monday when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) made his statement with regard to wheat and wheat surpluses and markets. He gave a comprehensive picture and put a good deal of information before the house. Those of us who have been around parliament hill for some time were prepared for a statement of that kind. He said that the initial price of wheat would be raised from 70 cents to 90 cents, and it had been generally believed that that was what would happen. When he made his statement in regard to the surpluses of wheat which the four great exporting countries of the world had on hand'-or the estimate of what they

would have on hand on July 31-it was a revelation to me, because the figure he gave was 1,300,000,000 bushels. That is a very considerable surplus.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) last night referred to Ontario wheat and said, "We should have a price equal to that paid for Ontario wheat," or something of that kind. Let me point out that Ontario wheat rose last fall owing to domestic markets, the demand that existed, and the shortage there was in wheat for the making of pastry flour. The domestic market forced up the price of wheat, and when it had reached a certain level the wartime prices and trade board put a ceiling on it. There is no ceiling on, western wheat. Western wheat is guaranteed merely a minimum price, and I hope that when the time comes and the price rises, as it is anticipated it will owing to markets for wheat, the board will not put the ceiling on too early.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) also gave a comprehensive statement regarding conditions generally in western Canada. He gave a good report on the plans they have this year for assisting western agriculture. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been in operation for some time, and also the acreage bonus policy. The statement he made, together with the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce looked very complete. I do not believe anyone had any serious objection to the statements made or the programme they mapped out for this year. Personally I considered it was quite far-reaching but that probably it was coming to western Canada. I did not anticipate speaking on the matter until one or two speeches were made that were rather provocative. So I felt I should say something in defence of Ontario agriculture.
As to what the future holds for wheat I would not even hazard a guess. Russia will probably be in the market for wheat in the near future. The great Ukraine area of 25 million acres will not be producing its normal crop this year, and it is quite probable that when the war is over, there will be a market in Russia for Canadian wheat. In the meantime Canada will have a big wheat surplus and be ready to meet any demand that may arise.
Wheat, I am sure, has been a major headache for the government. I think it was 1932 or 1933 when wheat in western Canada first became much of a problem. To help the situation the government started with a bonus of five cents a bushel. So wheat can scarcely be regarded as a war casualty. In 1938 western Canada harvested some 400 million bushels, and at 80 cents a bushel, which was a very low price then, it cost the treasury around

Wheat Board Act
$60 million to market that wheat. That was before the war, when all the markets of the world were open to Canadian wheat and wheat products.
I think it was the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) the other night who was comparing conditions on the farms in Ontario and in western Canada, and he made some references which to me were rather amusing. He spoke of the percentage of cars, radios, telephones and houses with running water installed. Comparisons are always odious, and to me that was a rather useless comparison, for it must be remembered that farming has been carried on in Ontario for at least one hundred years. Surely, after a century of farming, no one would begrudge 10 per cent of the farm homes having running water inside. As to telephones, if we had the same conditions as they have in western Canada, telephone subscribers a mile or two apart, I doubt if we would have telephones at all.
Ontario agriculture is not at all prosperous. I do not know what the 1941 census will show, but. the last census showed over $200 million of debt on the farms of this province. This means that around 50 per cent of the farms were mortgaged for approximately 50 per cent of their value. If anyone doubts that, let him get in touch with the farm loan board and he will find that is a fact. Some Ontario farms have been cultivated for two, three and four generations. The occupants have paid their debts and kept off relief, and I do not believe that western Canada begrudges them a little higher percentage of telephones or running water in the houses.
The farmer in western Canada has, we all admit, had difficulties. This is due largely to two reasons-one the loss of markets, and the other, partial, or in some places complete, crop failures. The government has been very generous in looking after the sufferers from those conditions and trying to alleviate the troubles of western Canada. Material assistance has been given through the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Apparently all parties are agreed that this has actually brought relief to those who were in need.
However, agriculture all over Canada has gone through difficult times. When this conflict is over and we come back to normal conditions again, if we are ever going to have parity prices in any degree-I do not like to talk about parity prices, for seldom can we recall when farm prices were on a parity basis -I believe we shall have to have a new agricultural policy for Canada if agriculture is to survive.
There are many agricultural problems in western Ontario. That is the reason why I am presenting a few thoughts this afternoon.

In southwestern Ontario there is a bean problem. It is only a minor problem compared with problems of the whole dominion, but beans have been grown in western Ontario for a number of years. Until recently they found a market readily in the British empire, but this year, due to war conditions, we have a surplus of beans to sell. The only market is the British empire, but I believe Britain is getting a great deal of her supply of beans from the United States under the lease-lend act and is not so anxious to take ours. They have, however, made a commitment to take ten thousand tons some time during the year. They are not dealing through our Canadian marketing service, but want to deal through the trade; that is, the British Ministry of Food apparently insists on dealing through the trade. That means we have a ceiling for beans in western Ontario for domestic sales; we have no ceiling for export. Therefore the exporters, of whom there are only two or three, are in a position for bargaining for -the beans to supply the British market at practically their own price. I know the Department of Agriculture is working on a plan to help the bean producers, in the hope of dealing directly through the marketing service of Canada. But if the bean producers of western Ontario were getting the same treatment to-day as the wheat producers, they would be -pretty well satisfied. How then can I go back, as representative of a riding like that, and ask the bean producers to be taxed to pay a bonus or subsidy to western wheat, when they cannot sell their own product?
We have also in western Ontario a sugar beet industry, as mentioned by the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Clark). A sugar beet refinery has been in operation in our riding for forty years. The price of sugar was set at the beginning of the war, and the growers' contracts were -based definitely on the sugar price. On the one hand the growers are faced with a rising labour cost while on the other the price of the product is pegged. The result is that one factory will probably close altogether, whereas in view of the fact that there is a shortage of sugar this year and a prospect of an even more acute shortage next year, we should be producing all we can. So I say, how can I, as representative of a riding which has a sugar -beet industry, go back and tell them that we want to tax them in order to pay a subsidy to the western wheat growers?
I am not very familiar with the wheat situation, but I should like to read a quotation from the hon. member for Wood Mountain
Wheat Board Act

(Mr. Donnelly) as reported at page 2422 of Hansard for April 29, 1941:
The farmer is getting the 85 cents a bushel; that is what this $35,000,000 is for.
That was the vote put through last year.
It will be seen that 230,000,000 bushels at 15 cents a bushel comes to $35,000,000. That is the 85 cents a bushel which the government is giving the farmer of western Canada. That is why the price is what it is, and where the 85 cents comes in.
In addition to that, which according to the hon. member's contention last year would raise the price of wheat to around 85 cents a bushel, after the session had been adjourned the government voted another $30,000,000 for prairie farm income. This, together with the $8,500,000 paid in prairie farm assistance I think would bring the price of western wheat close to $1 a bushel. Whether or not it worked out in that way I am not in a position to say, but that is my information for that statement. A little further on he said something else which was rather startling:
I say that wheat can be raised for 50 cents a bushel, and make no mistake about that. Profit can be made out of it at that price. It is being done and has been done during the past two years. It can he done; but it must be done on a mechanized farm. It must be done scientifically, and it cannot be done in an old-fashioned war. One can farm to-day 1,600 acres of wheat and not pay any more for his labour than he did a few years ago to farm 320 acres. I can grow 800 acres of wheat to-day with as little labour as I grew 100 acres a few years ago.
I am not in a position to say whether or not that is correct, but that was the statement made last year by the hon. member for Wood Mountain. I suppose there are over 250,000 farmers in western Canada, and some of them must have very large farms, for the other day the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) said he knew of some farm bonuses this year as large as $10,000. If that is not correct, the hon. member will tell me so, but that was what I understood him to say. What is the situation this year? The initial price is increased to 90 cents a bushel, No. 1 Fort William. This means an increased cost, in connection with the number of bushels they expect to buy, of around $56,000,000. Then the acreage bonus plan, if it is in the same category as last year, will cost another $30,000,000, and on top of that there will be perhaps another $10,000,000 in prairie farm assistance. Surely this will mean that the western farmer will get over $1 a bushel for his wheat this year.
I am not complaining that the farmers are getting too much for their wheat. I should like to see them get a great deal more, but
[Mr. H. A. MacKenzied
market conditions would not warrant it. The point that worries me, however, is whether they are satisfied with the assistance they are being given; and after having listened to what has been said in this house, I would say the answer was no. The other day the hon. member for Melfort made a statement which seemed very peculiar to me. As reported at page 1222 of Hansard he said:
I can assure you, sir, that is the attitude of western Canada. They are fed up and are desirous of getting a better deal than they have received in the past.
From western Canada we have also four other members of the cabinet-the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson), and the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar).
I need not read what followed immediately after that, because I think it better not to put it on record again, but a little further on the hon. gentleman continued:
We feel that if those members of the cabinet who represent western agriculture here were determined to get a fair deal for the western farmers, they could get it. In addition, we have thirty-four members supporting the government who belong to western Canada. If those members would stand up for the people they represent rather than for the party, they could obtain what western agriculture wants; and if the three sections together-the Prime Minister, the members of the cabinet, and the members supporting the government, assisted by the members on this side of the house from the west-made a united effort, we could get it *without a doubt.
I wonder whether it has ever dawned on the hon. member for Melfort that members of the cabinet represent Canada as a whole. Surely they must have a-national outlook, and surely they could not present something to the house that would) not be carried. If some of us would endeavour to get a more national outlook, and see beyond our own little domestic problems, we would get along with something really worth while. A little later the hon. gentleman said something that rather startled me. He spoke of some people who had moved from another part of Saskatchewan into his district, and said:
There are many people . . . who have moved to the northern part of Saskatchewan into the constituency which I represent. Many of those people are living on small farms; they took up bush homesteads and have some forty or fifty acres under cultivation. The wheat acreage reduction bonus does not mean a thing to them, neither does the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, because they always grow over twelve bushels to the acre, but their acreage is small. Neither does the other bill, which provides for a payment of 75 cents per acre on the cultivated acreage mean anything to them, because they have so little under cultivation.

Wheat Board Act
It appears that these people have reached the point where, if they cannot come under some scheme of bonus or assistance from the government, they cannot possibly help themselves. Here we have people who cannot come under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act because their crops are too good. They cannot come under the bonus scheme because they do not require that sort of assistance, and they have such a small acreage under cultivation that they must have some bonus or subsidy from the government or they cannot make a living. I should like to compare those farmers with some farmers in Ontario. Our people in Ontario have been farming under those conditions for many years, and paying much higher taxes. When this bill goes to committee I think we surely should insert a clause to take care of that little group of people in the hon. member's riding, who have such good crops that they do not need one form of assistance, in order that they may be given some subsidy or support of some kind. Such nonsense 1
Let me say further that when the income of western Canada was low the Minister of Agriculture-and I give him credit for it- sponsored a move to grant a subsidy or cost of living bonus to increase the income of prairie farms. Under that measure something like 75 cents an acre was paid on cultivated land up to a limit of 200 acres, which meant approximately $150 per farm.
Would the hon. gentleman allow me to ask a question? Is he aware that every farmer in Canada who is producing live stock as well as grain is receiving a bonus from the treasury?

I am aware of that fact. I am also aware that western Canada produces a great many cattle, and that every year Ontario buys many western cattle. But under that scheme another $30,000,000 was voted. No one is making any complaint about that; I give the minister credit for coming to their assistance. But I want to ask this: Has any member from western Canada risen in his place in this house and said how much they appreciate what has been done for them by the government?
Yes.

Well, I have not heard of it. I think they should at least give the government credit for having come to the assistance of the farmers of western Canada. I wonder whether they took part of the amount voted for prairie farm income to finance that delegation of two trainloads of farmers who came here to meet the Minister of Agriculture. Let me say that
the minister was in error the other day when he said that there had been no other delegations of farmers or farm organizations to see him. There have been small delegations.
I did not say that. There was one delegation here to see me yesterday morning, so I would not say that.

That was what I understood the minister to say. The fact remains, however, that small delegations . have come here to see him, but certainly our farmers could not finance a delegation amounting to two trainloads.
In conclusion, I say to my western friends that I have every sympathy for western Canada. I believe agriculture as a whole should be looked after, and looked after well, because for a long time it has not received its share from the point of view of revenue. I believe the western members who have been complaining so much should thank their lucky stars that the Minister of Agriculture is from western Canada, and has given them a great deal of assistance. They must appreciate, too, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is a western man. I believe those men are as fair as they can be, but a minister may be a little biased in favour of the constituency he represents.
I believe the whole economy is wrong. In my opinion the Minister of Trade and Commerce should come from one part of the country, and the Minister of Agriculture from another.
It was not much different when it was that way, before.

Well, it should be different. I believe the ministry must represent the whole dominion. We 245 members of the House of Commons come here with our problems, and those problems may look large to us. We lay them at the ministers' feet, or at the seat of government. We put them all together, and ask the government of the day to draw from that concoction a policy, not in the interests of western Canada, not in the interests of eastern Canada, but in the interests of all of Canada, and1 we ask them to be as fair and as equitable as possible. Sometimes we seem to take the position that because a minister lives in one particular spot he must fight for that spot, must get all the good things in life for it, or withdraw from the government.
I am not sure whether it was the hon. member for Battle "Axe"-or some such place -in western Canada, who placed a real gem in Hansard the other night. He pointed out that it was the squeaky wheel that got the
Wheat Board Act

grease and the crying baby who got the attention. I would change that a little and say that if the wheel which is getting the grease is still squeaking, we had better take the grease away from it, and give it something to squeak for.
Probably I have taken too much time, but may I repeat that I do not wish to be antagonistic. I do not believe I am, because I try to see the picture as a whole. We shall have plenty of time to fight over our domestic problems when this w'ar is over. I have not taken up much of the time of the house, but I believe we are spending far too much time in fighting about our wheat problem and the economics of our country, at a time when the empire is confronted with the greatest crisis in its history and is probably crumbling at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I believe my
years of experience on the farm, and my years of operating an elevator and as a grain buyer give me licence to speak on legislation of this kind. I feel inwardly gratified that my decision many years ago when I entered public life was that I would be more or less independent. After listening to some of the discussions I have heard in recent days I am thankful I made that decision. Therefore if, when speaking this afternoon, I say some things which may seem painful, I believe such statements necessary, and from my point of view I shall have to make them, no matter what party they may hurt.
May I say that I believe the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) would be well advised if he were to withdraw his amendment. In my opinion it is a futile gesture, if I may use that expression, and I suspect there is a little politics in it. Mr. Speaker, I absolutely refuse to play politics. If the hon. member will withdraw his amendment and allow the bill to go to the committee to which the other wheat bills have gone, I will promise him that in that committee I will fight along with him for what he is asking. For three or four years we have been criticizing the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for not submitting legislation of this kind to the inspection of the committee on agriculture. Now that we have got the minister to the point where he is willing to have the bills submitted to our scrutiny, let us jump at the chance to do so. Then, if we do not like what is done in committee we shall have our chance later in the house to express our opinions. My suggestion therefore would be that the hon. member withdraw his amendment, and I believe when the bill is given third reading we shall reach the same conclusion.
I should like to deal first with a matter which to my mind is serious. I refer to the statement of the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) that the Saskatchewan wheat pools had made dividends amounting to S3,000,000. He called it high finance, and added, "Remember, this is a

Wheat Board Act
cooperative company, and they do not pay any income tax." In my opinion that is a serious statement. The hon. member is not the first Liberal member I have heard express similar sentiments, and I wish to say now that if that is ever the policy of the Liberal party, do not expect to find me with that party.
I am a cooperator, and I belong to the Manitoba cooperative. In the dividends we are now earning we are just getting back the money we put into the stock of an institution which it was thought would help us in our farming, and lower our cost of production. Every dollar that was collected was deducted from some man's load of wheat. When he sold a carload of wheat, perhaps fifty dollars was deducted-which he otherwise would have had in his pocket-in order to build up a reserve to build an elevator. Now, when these men have reached the point where they are making dividends and there is a chance for them to get some of their original capital back, the suggestion is made that we tax these dividends. I do not think that would be right.
That is not the suggestion.
Absolutely.
The suggestion was-

Please, I would like not to have any interjections unless absolutely necessary. When the hon. member for Wood Mountain takes the stand that he is in favour of a reduction in elevator charges, I am with him. He is on solid ground there. The elevator charges are absolutely too high, and both he and I have been fighting those high charges for years. I have stood in this house, Mr. Speaker, session after session and pointed out-it might have seemed small but the principle was there just the same-that when we sell a carload of wheat containing 1,500 bushels we pay a service charge of $15, or 1 cent a bushel. When we sell a carload of barley, containing the same number of pounds, we pay the commission man $18.75. Is that fair? Anyone to whom I have spoken admits that it is not fair, but I never have heard any member of this house representing a farming district or any other district back me up when I made that plea. The barley industry is becoming more important every year, especially at this time. We may produce 200 million bushels of barley next year, and I believe the government would be well advised to have that commission charge- service charge is the technical name for itreduced to half a cent a bushel. It is not the first time that I have offered this suggestion and I am offering it again now.
The grain exchange sets the tariff for the commission charges. I have taken this matter up with the grain exchange. They say that the service charge on barley is a reasonable charge, and they absolutely refuse to change it. I have taken the matter up with the government. I can remember that a few years ago legislation went through this house to appoint a supervisor for the grain exchange with power to compel the brokers to produce their books for inspection. The bill went over to the other' house and was there so amended that it took away the right of the supervisor to scrutinize the brokers' figures. That emasculated the bill entirely, and I do not think a supervisor of the grain exchange has ever been appointed. Even if he were, he would have absolutely no power under that legislation. Why should an institution like the grain exchange be able to set their own tariffs and be able to charge $3.75 more for one car than they charge for another containing the same number of pounds? I say it is time the government stepped in and showed them the rules.
The hon. member for Wood Mountain referred to an article which he saw in a financial paper. I have it here, and I think I should read it and put it on the records of this house. It is an editorial in the Financial Post of February 14, 1942, and says:
Saskatchewan wheat pool profits last year amounted to almost $3 millions after the usual depreciation. Had the pool been an ordinary private grain company the public treasury would have been enriched to the extent of over $1-5 million in income and excess profit taxes. But being classed as a "cooperative", the pool paid exactly nothing.
The prairie wheat pools are competing directly with private grain companies which must and do pay full national taxes. They are performing a service not one whit different from that of their competitors. Long before this the dominion Department of Finance should have stepped in, ended this absurd and unfair discrimination, and stopped a very substantial leakage in taxes.
That really is the serious part of the statement made by the hon. member for Wood Mountain. I am just a little nervous that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) might endeavour to seek a new avenue whereby he would get some taxation. I do not think it would be fair to go to this source.

They have to pay
income tax.

I am very glad to see my hon. friend back in the house. I missed him from his usual front seat. No; we should not

have to pay taxes because we are only getting our own money back. The hon. member for Wood Mountain also said that he belonged to the pool.
Sure.
Oh, what loyalty 1
I shall have to tell you something about it.

I have heard' of people
damning an institution with faint praise, but a man who belongs to an institution and then gives to the house the information the hon. member for Wood Mountain gave the other day-I say that is not loyalty.
I am in favour of $1 a bushel being paid for our wheat. That is nothing new for me; I advocated it here in a speech I made in the house last fall, on November 19, 1941. At that time I believed we could pay $1 a bushel and limit the deliveries to any quantity which the government thought it could sell-if not 230 million bushels, limit it to 200 million bushels. That factor could be absolutely controlled. The bonus I did not like then; I do not like it now and perhaps never will. I must qualify that because I think the Prairie Farm Assistance Act does act as a crop insurance policy, and the other act, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, has the effect of conserving the fertility of the soil. I think there is some merit in both those acts. But the wheat acreage reduction bonus, and the from income bonus, which was the best of them all, would have been unnecessary if the farmers had received a high enough price for their wheat. Then we could have done without them.
The farmers want legislation that they can understand, and I think the Minister of Agriculture will agree with me when I say that they do not understand this legislation. The minister understands it, but I must confess that I do not.
In my part of the country the farmers do not want this bonus plan. I make that statement positively, believing that I am stating the absolute truth. But they took advantage of It-I am talking of the wheat acreage reduction bonus-in order to get some income which was denied them because the price of wheat was too low. But it upset their whole routine, and they turned all sorts of corners in order to get a little summer-fallowing in here, put barley in there, and so on.
I have a letter here which expresses the mind, I think, of most of the people in my district. This gentleman is of Liberal stock, a very open-minded man. In fact he was a candidate in the last provincial election. He is a man of good intelligence, and since the

intelligence of my constituency is fairly high, I think it well worthwhile for me to read part of his letter. First he expresses his opinion that the initial price should be $1 a bushel. Then he goes on to say:
Of course I won't be greatly surprised at a guaranteed price of less than $1. What I really expect is some complicated plan that no one can thoroughly understand until it is too late to do anything about it.
That is typical of the opinion of the farmers in my district. I have stated that I dio not like the bonus. I think that one of the worst features of the bonus is its inequality. Fifty per cent of the farmers of Manitoba sow less than fifty acres of wheat. The figures I quote are based on the 1935 census. I tried to get them up to date, but the bureau does not have them. I believe that in Alberta the percentage is forty-two per cent. Even in Saskatchewan, twenty-five per cent of the farmers sow less than fifty acres of wheat. There were 187,000 farmers in the western provinces, including, I assume, the Peace River district, who made application for the wheat reduction bonus. I asked the minister a question on -this point during his speech, when he said he would rather not be interrupted ; in any event he did not answer. I just wished to know how many farmers there are in the three prairie provinces. I have since ascertained from one of his officials, although this is only an estimate, that there are 290,000. And 187,000 made application! This means that 103,000 farmers in that western country did not get any of this wheat reduction bonus.
Many of that number are market gardeners.

Many of them are very small farmers. Then the -man who did not produce wheat in 1939 and 1940 was out of the picture -altogether. We have in Manitoba lots of men who have not been growing wheat for five or six years.
Mr. GARDINER; There are also the -ranchers.

There was no chance for these men to share in the wheat -bonus. So you get -back to the principle that if you pay the higher price for a limited number of bushels you are going to benefit them all- the big farmer as well as the smaller farmer.
We heard rumours that the Liberals from Saskatchewan, headed by our Minister of Agriculture, put up a tremendous fight to have the government recognize this increase in prices and the continuance of the minister's programme. I think -they did pretty well. I believe that every Liberal member from Saskatchewan would put up -the best fight he

knew how; and, knowing the Minister of Agriculture as I do, I am confident that he also would put forth his very best efforts. But I wonder where were the Liberals from Alberta?
Hear, hear.

I
can tell the hon. member where the Liberals of Alberta were.
These are rumours. I am asking -the question, if the Liberal members from Alberta were there.

Not at this meeting
that I am talking about? Well, then, were the Liberal members from Manitoba there? I was not there. I would have been delighted to be there upholding their hands and battling at their side. Perhaps, if the Liberal members from Manitoba and from Alberta had been there, we would have got $1 wheat. We should have been there.

You should all have been there.
