I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson); all the western members should have been there, and all hon. members who were interested. But did the leader of the opposition practise what he preaches? I don't think he ever did. I as an independent member can make these statements, believing that we should get what we are entitled to.
It was the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) who made that observation. I agree with him.
Was the grain exchange represented there?

The government policy is reasonably good. But I do not think they should take all the credit. There is a war on, and that has something to do, it seems to me,
with the increased prices which agriculturists are getting. I say that without wishing to detract one iota from the effort of the government; in some respects I think it has been very good. Now they are granting us 90 cents a bushel for wheat, and, according to the Minister of Agriculture's own figures, that is 57 cents a bushel less than parity price based on the period 1926-29. The barley price on the same basis was 73 cents, and the government is setting a floor price at 60 cents, which means that it is 13 cents less than the parity price of 1926-29. Eor oats the parity price was 59 cents, and the government is putting a floor price of 45 cents, leaving 14 cents of a spread between the parity price and the government price. The floor prices for the coarse grains, are, of course, a consideration; they really do mean something.
Here is where I am going to say something which may be painful but is, I believe, necessary. The difficulty with regard to Manitoba is that our leader is apparently more interested in the grain trade than in the welfare of our farmers. I am very sorry that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) is not in his seat. I know him better, perhaps, than any other man in this house.
He is ill this afternoon.

I am sorry that that is so, but it is not my fault; whether he is here or whether he is not, I intend to make this statement. I am not actuated by any political motives; I am actuated by the desire to serve my people; and when I look over the years during which the minister has sat in this house and review the attitude he has taken on the grain question, I believe that what I have to say to-day should have been said before. When you make a charge you should be able to substantiate it; that is why I used the word "apparently". I am now going to define my meaning.
When the grain act was being revised, in 1925, the present Minister of Mines and Resources was definitely behind the practice of mixing our wheat. I have not time to go into that, but to me the picture is so familiar that I can almost see the old house as it stood, and hear the discussion which took place at that time. He was absolutely behind the mixing of wheat. He turned round to the other Progressive members and said, "I am sorry I must appear at variance with my colleagues from western Canada, but they do not represent the opinion of western Canada".

Wheat Board Act

There we had the spectacle of our farm leader voting by himself, while all the other Progressive members supported the proposal for the non-mixing of wheat.
Again, he was mainly responsible for the taking away of the right of the farmer to name the terminal of his choice. I do not want to go at length into that, but he was the one man who took away that right from the farmer. He declared at that time, that technically it was not a right, but it was the system which we were working under, an actual right we enjoyed, whether we had the legal right or not. He made it absolutely sure that we could not designate our own terminal elevator unless we released the country elevator from the loss which might be sustained if they shipped the carload of wheat to any other terminal. He had his eye at that very time on the pool elevators, especially the one at the head of the lakes. In recent legislation he has invariably spoken in defence of the grain trade.
I have on this note of mine the pages where this information will be found in Hansard. It will be found on page 2537 of Hansard of 1940. We all remember-those of us who were here in 1939-when Mr. Motherwell named him as the opponent of the wheat board. Then he went to Great Britain and returned with the advice that Britain wanted the grain exchange to function. He was interested in the grain exchange, notwithstanding the fact that the market was closed in Britain and they had sent an agent, and all that they purchased was purchased through that agency. Yet he came back saying that the old country wished the grain exchange to be kept open in Winnipeg to set the price of wheat. He opposed the government in the policy of making an advance on farmer-held grain. We know that he said in this house, when asked by some hon. members whether he was in favour, "If you ask me, it is only moonshine." The Minister of Agriculture knows whether I am right in saying that he went with him to Winnipeg to represent the government, to confer with him on the wheat board, to see whether an advance would be made to farmer-stored wheat, and the decision was made that no government advance would be given.
No; he was not sent with me.
He was there at your meeting.
He was in Winnipeg and I came from Regina.
It was quite a coincidence. Why split hairs?
We were both there on the invitation of the premier of Manitoba. There was no arrangement at all other than that.
Will the Minister of Agriculture say he is jointly responsible?
I will say, Mr. Speaker, that I was largely responsible for the decision which was made at that meeting as far as the government is concerned.

Then I will include the
Minister of Agriculture in this latter charge.
I still think I was right.

What a different policy from what is taking place now in the United States 1 I have here a letter-I shall not have time to read it-from a man in charge there who tells me that the policy of granting advances to farmers in the United States is this, that they store their grain in a granary after meeting the specifications of the government inspector, and that it has had the effect of building many thousands of granaries throughout that country. That is where we want our wheat held-on the farms and not in the elevator, costing us $50,000,000 a year.
By far the greater part of that wheat in the United States is in elevators and not on farms.

I hope, Mr. Speaker, you are keeping track of the time I am losing. Further, the Minister of Mines and Resources declared that the present tariffs were fair to the elevator companies in the face of the demand for lower storage charges. What does the hon. member for Wood Mountain think of that? You will find it at page 2379 of Hansard of 1940. The minister was never friendly to the wheat pool! If you want that information look at page 2268 of Hansard of 1940 and page 2272 of the same year.
Let me now say something about the delegation which presented the brief here in Ottawa. In the first place, I wish to congratulate the people of Saskatchewan upon sending that delegation to Ottawa. They got subscriptions from 1S5.000 signers and the expenses were paid out of the joint collection of 24 cents from each individual signer. That is how it was paid. Their journey to Ottawa, however, was ridiculed by the Minister of Agriculture, who asked, where will they get the money? It was condemned by many of our papers also. But after they came here and presented their brief they were commended by the minister and by the press in general. They made what they thought and what we all thought was a very favourable

Wheat Board Act
impression. The minister himself has told us that it was not a delegation of farmers, that they were reeves of municipalities and mayors of cities. I say it was a delegation representative of the whole of Saskatchewan. After their brief was presented the government promised them consideration. This is what they asked for: The delegation's proposal was that they be paid $1 a bushel initial price for what quantity of wheat the government thought they could take, and that was 41 cents, or, to be exact, 41-7 cents, below the parity price of 1926 and 1929.
Was that not a reasonable request? Do you not think it was a generous compromise? I do. Then they favoured restricted deliveries and said that those surpluses which could not be purchased should be taken care of by the farmers back on their farms. The policy of this government should be to encourage that, because there is nothing that will convince the farmer more than, when he sees his bin full of wheat which he cannot sell, to be told that he should grow something else besides wheat; and you would relieve the taxpayers of the country by not paying storage charges. I am not advocating storage for the farmer. Let him build his own granary to store his wheat, and when it is wanted he can take out the wheat and sell it. If he cannot sell it he will not grow wheat, and that is very good logic.
This higher price of $1 a bushel will not increase the production of wheat. That is a fallacy. You have all the machinery in your hands to control that. Do you think the farmer is crazy enough to grow something he cannot sell? He is not going to grow it.
I come now to the presentation of the farm organization, which represented the whole of the dominion, and in that connection I wish to read this paragraph of their brief:
The general nature of our organization is, of course, known to you. We have made substantial progress during the last year in the consolidation of our provincial units and we now have an affiliated membership of more than
350.000	farmers.
It is growing. We are growing. We shall get to the point where we shall have double
350.000	presenting briefs, and they will be listened to. They listened in this case-I am giving credit for that. They said that their first consideration, their paramount duty, was to use all their efforts in the prosecution of the war, and then, speaking for the whole of the dominion, they said that they would like to have a voice in formulating the farm policies of Canada. That should be appreciated by the government, and I believe it is. May I quote the following:
44561-84}
All of the member bodies of this federation from western Canada are on record to the effect that the basic price for the coming year should be not less than $1 per bushel basis No. 1 northern at lakehead or seaboard terminals. This represents widespread opinion in western Canada and further evidence will be given in the presentation by the delegation from the province of Saskatchewan which is to meet the government this afternoon. We can assure the government that opinion in Manitoba and in Alberta is equally strong and that such a request has also the support of the agricultural interests in other parts of Canada represented by this association.
I believe the government of Saskatchewan endorsed their representations in to to. There, Mr. Speaker, you have the representations as made by the organized farmers of this dominion.
One of the mistakes made last year in the submission to the Minister of Agriculture by the organized farmers of Canada was that they did not propose a definite price. It was generally agreed that the price should be 85 cents, but they did not state that in their presentation. The Minister of Agriculture, taking advantage of that, made a statement which is found on page 1923 of Hansard for March 27, 1941. He said:
_ The fact that neither the Saskatchewan pool in its recommendations, nor the advisory committee in its recommendations, nor the Canadian agricultural federation in its recommendations, was able to insert a price, I think clearly indicates that, while there may have been some sentiment in these organizations in favour of changing the advance provided for in the wheat board act, there was considerable sentiment against it.
I submit to the minister that they certainly 'have asked a definite price this year. They profited by the mistake they made last year. They have asked for a dollar a bushel initial price at the lake head, backed by the organized farmers of Canada, and I think they are entitled to it.
With the exception of the two acts which I mentioned previously, they are willing to forgo the wheat acreage reduction bonus and the farm income bonus if the government will raise the price to $1 a bushel. This would cost the taxpayers less than it would to pay these bonuses and 90 cents.
Plus what is required to bring it to parity.

Why does the government not adopt the policy which would satisfy 90 per cent of the farmers of western Canada? Perhaps I am putting that too strongly-at any rate 90 per cent of the farmers of Manitoba.

The suggestion the hon. member is making is that the farmers asked

for only $1 a bushel. But in fact they asked for $1 a bushel plus enough to bring it up to parity. The comparison should be made between those two things.
They are asking for $1 a bushel initial price. Why hedge it around with these other things? They do not like your bonuses.
Seven hundred in your municipality applied for them.
They applied1 because they needed the money. It upset their whole farming routine. We should not do that.
Would they have got the money in any other way, except through the bonus?

Yes. They were asking for
85-cent wheat last year; that would have provided about as much money as the bonuses. They do not like the bonus. They like the higher initial payment.
It has been said in western Canada that it is because of opposition from Ontario and other parts of eastern Canada that it was not granted. I do not believe it. If the government would come out boldly for a policy of $1 a bushel, those hon. members would be found supporting us. I asked an hon. member from Ontario who was here a moment ago what he got for his wheat in Ontario this year. He said $1.05 at the bam. We have to haul our wheat to the elevator as well as pay the charges. I know that Canadians are willing to grant justice to other parts of Canada. I do not believe that Ontario is opposed to a higher initial price.
Let me quote from a dispatch from Regina of April 9, 1941. It is headed:
Taggart says Eastern Opinion Influenced Government Wheat Policy.
The dispatch reads:
Widespread belief in eastern Canada that the west was determined to "get all we can from the government and pay nothing back" had a definite effect in determining the 1941 wheat policy of the federal government, declared Hon. J. G. Taggart, Saskatchewan Minister of Agriculture, yesterday.
I do not believe that is true. You can hardly speak to a man on the streets of Ottawa who has not a son or a nephew or an uncle or a daughter in western Canada. They are our own people.

Does the hon. member
know what he could get for wheat in Manitoba by feeding it to hogs, as we do in Ontario?

The experience of one of
the best feeders we have in Manitoba is that he can get $1 a bushel for wheat by feeding it to hogs.

* Mr. FURNISS: Yes, at his farm. That is right.

But you cannot feed to
hogs all the wheat that is grown in western Canada.
How many hogs would you have if you fed all the western wheat crop to hogs?

I believe my time has
expired-
Go on.

No, thank you; I do not
think I should continue. I have said enough to indicate my position and what I shall do in regard to this legislation when it comes before the house for third reading. I am not particular as to whether I vote for the amendment or against it. I still believe it would be wise to withdraw it. I believe it is a futile gesture, and that it smacks of politics, if that is a proper word.

That is not
fair.

Perhaps it is not, but I have that suspicion, and feeling as I do I cannot vote for the amendment. It really does not make any difference. But I shall be here with both feet if we do not get that $1 a bushel which was asked by these farm organizations and will vote against the government on third reading. I am not going to fail these organizations. That is where they get their bread and butter. The loyalty I owe is not to any political party; it is to the people on the farms, both east and west, whom I represent in this house. I represent not only the constituency of Portage la Prairie in Manitoba, but in this particular case I represent the agriculturists of western Canada.

order. Standing order 35 provides:
When two or more members rise to speak, Mr. Speaker calls upon the member who first rose in his place; but a motion may be made that any member who has risen "be now heard", or "do now speak", which motion shall be forthwith put without debate.
I submit respectfully that I rose from my seat three times this afternoon and according to the rules of the house I must have the floor.

It is true that the hon.
member did rise, but he knows that I have a list of the members who it has been arranged

should speak to-day, and who are all present. I saw the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Marshall) when he rose in his place to take the floor, and he now has the floor. If the hon. member is dissatisfied he has the right under the rule he has just cited-or someone may do it for him-to move that he be now heard. If any hon. member rises in his place and requests that the hon. member be now heard, I shall put it to the house and the house will then decide who shall speak. The hon. member for Camrose has the floor.

I rise to another point
of order. Nothing in the standing orders of the house mentions the lists of the whips of any party. It is absolutely against the rules of the house to follow those lists. I stand upon these regulations and ask that I be allowed to speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: On the point of order raised by the hon. member, the rule has been established for many years that the Speaker sees a certain hon. member in debate; and frequently in the British House of Commons some members wait for weeks before they get the privilege of taking part in the debate. It is not at all a matter of the whips' lists, but in order to expedite the work of the house some arrangement must be made between those responsible for the conduct of the house. The Speaker has the right to see any hon. member he chooses to see; that has been part of our system for centuries.

What has been said by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) is in accordance with the practice of this house, and I do not see how we could very well depart from it as a general principle, for the reasons which have been stated. On the other hand, however, there should be a sense of fairness in regard to this matter. If the whips choose to make up lists-which of course are not official in any way-and hand them to the Speaker, who follows the lists and sees only those whose names are contained therein, I could conceive of a situation where an hon. member might never be heard, and of course that would be a denial of justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That has never happened in this house.

Well, we had the inception of it right here this afternoon. I hold no brief for the hon. member who is endeavouring to catch the eye of the Speaker, but I have an innate sense of justice which tells me that this is not exactly right. It is near the end of the afternoon, of course,
and in a few moments we are going to adjourn. I do suggest that some arrangement be made by the whips-and this may be a means of expediting it-whereby the hon. member may be able to express his views on the floor of this house in regard to the question now before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: May I point out to my hon. friend that the hon. member already has been told that he can speak in this debate on Monday.
I had not been told that. I do not know why he did not agree to that arrangement.

The hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) knows the rules of the house, I am sure. With what has been said by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) I am entirely in agreement. I want to see that every hon. member has the opportunity to speak, as he is entitled to do; but I do think the Chair should not be placed in the position of having to discriminate between hon. members on both sides of the house. With the present composition of the house I should be bound to make mistakes and to discriminate unfairly. The rules provide, however, that if the hon. member is dissatisfied he may, through some other hon. member, ask that he be heard. If that is done I will put it to the house, which will judge as to who should be heard. In this instance no one has asked that the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains be heard; therefore the hon. member for Camrose has the floor.

Then, following the
remarks of the leader of the opposition, I ask the Chair to give me the floor.

The hon. member must understand that I have already given my ruling. The standing order is there; it can be taken advantage of by the hon. member. As soon as that is done it will be brought before the house, and the house will decide as to who is to speak. In this case no such request has been made to the Chair; therefore I have seen the hon. member for Camrose, who now has the floor.
Mr. Speaker, I appeal from your decision.
Mr. Speaker-
Mr. Speaker, I have said that I appeal from your decision.

No one has stood up. Five members must rise, and no one has risen except the hon. member himself. The hon. member for Camrose will now proceed.

First I should like to pay my humble respects to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) for the fine courage he displayed this afternoon in championing the cause of the farmer. His splendid exposition was commendable. One thing he does not lack is courage.
I have a little problem, Mr. Speaker, which I should like to share with you. If an Irishman speaks on Bill No. 13 on Friday, March 13, at 5.45 o'clock, does it bode ill for the bill or for the Irishman? I think in checking the time, and considering the difficulty I have experienced in getting the floor, that the Irishman has lost the first round.
When I last spoke in this house, on Bill No. 5, I emphasized the importance of having an objective or goal toward which we must strive with persistence and courage. The solution of the difficulties of agriculture is as vital to Canada as the placing of returned men in industrial positions at the conclusion of this war or an increase in the pensions given to old age pensioners. We must assess correctly the problems of agriculture; for until we do their solution is impossible. Over four hundred people, representing all shades of public opinion and all classes of society, travelled from Saskatchewan to Ottawa a short time ago to present a petition at the seat of government. This petition, signed by over
180,000	people, proposed a new deal for agriculture. It is not my intention to discuss the petition, but similar proposals were advanced by the legislatures of the three western provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, as well as by all sorts of farm organizations such as the National Council of Agriculture, the United Farmers of Alberta, the United Farmers of Canada, various grain companies, many boards of trade and chambers of commerce. Still the wishes of these various bodies and of such a vast number of people engaged in all kinds of agriculture in western Canada have been thwarted. Let me hasten to state that I do not altogether blame the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for the mess agriculture is in to-day, nor do I absolve him entirely from all responsibility; for after all, he must assume some of that responsibility. Cabinet ministers as a general rule do not frame policies; they are too busy. Policies are framed by the real rulers of this country, the bureaucrats. These bureaucrats are the people who formulate the plans, who draw up the policies, and who submit these plans and policies together with recommendations to the minister. We never get to know very much about these same bureaucrats, because they assume no responsi-

bility; they are never dismissed from office. If their plans turn out to be worthless they are not even admonished.
As I have said before in the house, and as I shall say on many future occasions, these individuals have power but they have no responsibility. They have one eye firmly fixed on the Department of Finance and the other eye on the job they have in hand. They are constantly hedged in by financial restriction. And I say this, Mr. Speaker, that if you are looking for the real saboteurs of agriculture to-day you will find them not in the Department of Agriculture but rather in the Department of Finance. These bureaucrats have not yet given heed to the Minister of Finance who has uttered the words, "What is physically possible shall be made financially possible". This expression, by the way, which we have heard so often, and which has been adopted by the Minister of Finance, was pirated from Major Douglas, the founder of the social credit philosophy.
I believe we are going about this whole problem in the wrong way. We farmers have not yet decided what our objective or our goal should be, and we are suggesting to the government methods whereby some goal might be attained concerning which we as individuals have not yet reached a decision. I say therefore that we must first decide what we want, and then leave the government free to perfect the plan which will make our suggestions capable of accomplishment. Farmers not only in western Canada but in eastern Canada are, in my opinion, faced with two problems; first, debt and its twin evil, taxation, and, second, the exhaustion of the fertility of the soil.
With respect to number one I am not going to say very much. Through a series of crop failures, combined with persistent low prices, in the last ten years farmers have gone further and further into debt. Taxes have steadily mounted, and this has been brought about because municipalities-and I know whereof I speak-have been compelled to accept responsibility for many new things, such as indigent relief, mothers' allowances, old age pensions, hospitalization and the payment of doctors' bills.
With regard to the second problem, namely, the exhaustion of the fertility of the soil, I would say that under present conditions, by ignorant or unscrupulous exploitation and exhaustion of fertility vast profits have been made by financial interests-not by the farmers-in the name of cheap food. The chief characteristic of real farming is that it is a way of life rather than a business. I would therefore say that the goal toward

Questions
which all organizations connected with agriculture should steadfastly strive are these: (1) a complete solution of the debt problem and its twin evil, taxation, and (2) the restoration of agriculture to its proper function, namely, a way of life rather than a profitable or unprofitable industry.
